column2: ETSI TS 104 275 V1.1.1: Securing Artificial Intelligence (SAI); Application of Baseline Cyber Security Requirements for AI Models and Systems principles to Generative AI; Preventing Harm from Deepfakes
column7: - AI differs from traditional software through risks such as data poisoning, model obfuscation, and indirect prompt injection, plus differences in how data is managed. · - Deepfakes have been used to sway elections and to create non-consensual pornography, child sexual abuse material, low-cost deepfake adverts, and synthetic terrorist content. · - Deepfake harm falls into three groups: psychological (extortion, defamation), financial (identity theft, fraud, stock manipulation), and societal (election manipulation, national security). · - The harms, threats, and mitigations that apply to GenAI also apply to Agentic AI, which the specification treats as an evolution of GenAI. · - Simple changes to how a deepfake is produced can sharply cut detector reliability, and compression on social platforms removes the pixels and artefacts detectors depend on. · - Manual deepfake detection by a skilled reviewer works for small volumes but cannot keep up with the volume of audio-visual material shared today. · - Victims of non-consensual deepfakes see the same content reappear on many sites and have to request formal removal each time.
column8: - System Operators and Developers shall give users training on GenAI deepfake threats; the conformance test fails if that training content was not reviewed in the last 12 months. · - The GenAI user interface shall encourage responsible use through content filters, clear labels on AI-generated content, and notices about limits on output reliability and accuracy. · - Operators and Developers shall complete a risk assessment and implement and verify required mitigations before a GenAI system is deployed, with residual risks documented and approved. · - Operators and Developers shall keep human oversight of a deployed GenAI system, monitor it, and implement tracked updates when risks materialize. · - Developers, Operators, and Data Custodians shall get informed consent before training or adapting GenAI on a user's works, and the system shall enforce opt in or opt out at any time. · - The Developer shall confirm that GenAI training data was legally accessed or licensed; incomplete data lineage or missing license evidence fails conformance. · - An organization shall have a risk communication policy that covers its roles, statutory duties, escalation paths, and information sharing with authorities such as a Market Surveillance Authority.
column9: - Continuous risk research: System Operators and Developers review safety and security research on a set cadence, for example quarterly and not only after incidents, and track decisions, owners, and actions. · - Multilingual red teaming: Developers and System Operators send the same harmful prompt in several languages and add controls when any version produces harmful output. · - Cross-verification: System Operators and Developers check GenAI outputs against trusted external sources, and the human oversight process responds to incorrect outputs and hallucinations. · - Infringement testing: the Developer generates sample images or text, runs reverse image or text searches for infringing matches, and adds measures to stop repeats. · - Security transparency: Developers and System Operators tell GenAI users what steps they take to secure infrastructure and the supply chain. · - Patch notification: Developers and System Operators keep a policy that informs users about security updates, patches, and threat mitigations as they are applied. · - Privacy-preserving training: developers apply federated learning, differential privacy, and model anonymization where anonymization does not compromise the model's intended purpose. · - Data subject rights at end of life: Developers and System Operators set up processes that honor end-user GDPR rights of access (Art. 15), erasure (Art. 17), and portability.
